resources.string: María de Molina (1264–1321) was one of the most important women in the history of Castile as she dedicated her life to maintaining peace and stability in the kingdom. She was queen, mother of a king, and grandmother of a king, but above all a prudent and respected ruler who knew how to gain the support of the people and nobility in difficult times.
She was born around 1264, probably near the monastery of Santa María de Palazuelos located between the current Corcos del Valle and Cabezón de Pisuerga.

María belonged to a noble and powerful family. She was the daughter of Alfonso de Molina, brother of King Fernando III, and Mayor Alfonso de Meneses. From a young age, she grew up surrounded by the political life of the Castilian court. Her education prepared her to assume responsibilities, learning to read, write, and understand the affairs of the kingdom, something uncommon for women of her time.

In 1282 she married the infante Sancho, future king Sancho IV. Their marriage was not well received by everyone: they were close relatives and needed a papal dispensation that took years to arrive. Nevertheless, María accompanied her husband in the toughest moments, even when his right to the throne was questioned. After the death of her father-in-law Alfonso X, Sancho was crowned king and she became queen of Castile.

During the reign of Sancho IV (1284–1295), María actively participated in political decisions. She gained fame as an intelligent, prudent, and just woman. She accompanied the king on campaigns and defended the legitimacy of her family against internal enemies of the kingdom. Her reign was marked by struggles between nobles and the consolidation of the Castilian monarchy.
The regencies of María de Molina

After the death of her husband Sancho IV in 1295, María assumed the regency for her son Fernando IV, who was only nine years old. With prudence and firmness, she managed to keep the crown amidst internal conflicts, earning the respect of nobles and councils. Years later, in 1312, she governed again as regent for her grandson Alfonso XI, once again demonstrating her wisdom and ability to maintain peace and unity in the kingdom in difficult times.

María de Molina is remembered as one of the great queens of Castile for her political capacity and sense of justice. She founded and supported numerous monasteries, such as Las Huelgas in Valladolid, where she was buried. She promoted education, religion, and peace in times of war. Her figure symbolizes prudence, loyalty, and the defense of the common good.

Pasos de María is an educational and interactive guide dedicated to spreading the life and legacy of María de Molina, as well as showcasing the historical heritage of Valladolid. The application offers detailed descriptions, images, schedules and locations of points of interest, map routes, content adapted for young audiences, and the option to take quizzes individually and in multiplayer mode. The individual test feature has a password that will be provided by the teachers, so that students cannot learn the questions before taking the quiz in multiplayer mode, but can later reinforce their knowledge on their own. 
 Its goal is to provide access to local history in a didactic and visual way, and in a more modern format that can further spark the interest of young people; the data has been compiled from historical and cultural sources. The application was created for the Santa María La Real de Huelgas School.

 Application created by Miguel Bueno González, Gonzalo José Colina Báscones and Daniel Fernández García

The Royal Alcázar of Valladolid (12th–13th centuries), located at the western end of the medieval town near the confluence of the northern branch of the Esgueva with the Pisuerga, was a fortified and palatial complex composed of two enclosures: the alcazarejo (or old alcázar), on the lower terrace by the Esgueva river, and the main alcázar, on the higher terrace near the parish of San Julián. After centuries of royal use and several reforms, it was donated to the Benedictines in 1390. Its remains are today integrated into the Monastery of San Benito el Real and the Patio Herreriano Museum, where traces of the old complex can still be seen. The alcazarejo had a roughly square plan — about 31 metres per side according to excavations — and featured eight solid towers: one in the middle of each curtain wall and one at each corner.
Collegiate Church of Santa María la Mayor

The Collegiate Church of Santa María la Mayor of Valladolid was first built in a Romanesque version in the late 11th century (around 1180) by order of Count Pedro Ansúrez. Later, in the 1220s, Don Juan Domínguez Medina, abbot of the collegiate church, ordered the demolition of the primitive Romanesque temple to build a new proto-Gothic one, preserving only the original tower. Over subsequent centuries it underwent other transformations. Today only one of the entrance gates remains.
Church of Santa María de la Antigua

The Church of Santa María de la Antigua in Valladolid is a Romanesque church from the 12th century, completed in Gothic style. From the 12th century it retains the tower and a portico. The tower, with a height close to 50 m and topped with a spire, is the tallest Romanesque bell tower in Spain. The rest of the building is Gothic and neo-Gothic, possibly rebuilt in the 14th century under Alfonso XI of Castile, with notable influences from the Cathedral of Santa María in Burgos.
C. del Arzobispo Gandasegui, s/n, 47002 Valladolid

The original church was located at the centre of the current San Miguel Square. It was first dedicated to Saint Pelayo and changed to San Miguel in the mid-12th century. A document dated 18 January 1151 already refers to it as the Church of Saint Michael, and it is considered the oldest parish in Valladolid. In 1478 the original church burned down and was rebuilt in the same place by order of the Catholic Monarchs at the end of the 15th century. During the fire all the city documents kept there were lost.
Old Hermitage of Santa María Magdalena

It was built on one of the gates of the old city wall, located on the outskirts in the area later called Prado de la Magdalena, which in those centuries was countryside and orchards. This small chapel retained its original appearance until 1538, when a funerary chapel ordered by Doctor Corral, auditor of the Royal Chancery and member of the Royal Council, was added — securing a prominent burial place. After the extension, the larger Renaissance/Gothic church was built.

The current Plaza Mayor of Valladolid was originally known as the Plaza del Mercado because in the Middle Ages the town\'s central market was held there. According to documents, a market was already located there in 1260. In the Middle Ages the square was an open space outside the walls or at the town boundary where the main market was established: meat, fish, vegetables and other products were sold. Over time trade was organised into guild streets around the square — for example, the Lingerie Street or the Torners Street — reflecting the artisanal and commercial activity surrounding the market. In September 1561 a great fire destroyed much of the square\'s surroundings, which led to urban reorganization.

Valladolid, located at the confluence of the Esgueva and the Pisuerga rivers, had since the Middle Ages its main river crossing over the Pisuerga — the so-called Major Bridge — which connected the town with settlements on the other bank and favoured the emergence of the La Victoria neighbourhood. Local tradition attributes the construction of a stone bridge to Doña Eylo, wife of Pedro Ansúrez, in the late 11th century (around 1080), probably over an earlier wooden crossing; however, most visible parts of the current bridge date from later construction phases (13th–14th centuries), and the attribution to Eylo belongs more to legend than to archaeological certainty.
Monastery of Santa Maria de Palazuelos

The origin of the monastery is linked to the lineage of the lords of Meneses. In 1213 Alfonso Téllez de Meneses received the town of Palazuelos from Alfonso VIII as a reward for his participation in the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa. Later, Alfonso Téllez and his wife ceded those lands to the Cistercian convent of San Andrés de Valvení so it could move there. In 1313 the councils of Castile met in this monastery to establish the regency of the young king Alfonso XI. María was born around 1264 in a place near the monastery of Santa María de Palazuelos, situated between the current Corcos del Valle and Cabezón de Pisuerga. It is a Cistercian monastic complex in a transitional style from Romanesque to Gothic: sober, austere, with little ornamentation, massive ashlar walls and large vaults. The church has a basilica plan, three naves of four spans and an east-oriented apse with three chapels: the central one with a polygonal apse and the lateral ones semicircular, a feature uncommon in Cistercian monasteries.

The palace was a royal residence, including King Sancho IV of Castile and his wife María de Molina, on a site adapted as a royal residence in the 13th century. After Sancho IV\'s death in 1295, his widow María de Molina acted as regent and faced political conflict that led to reinforcement of the palace\'s security, turning it into a fortified enclosure. Over time the buildings were abandoned or repurposed. Most of the palace finally disappeared, and today only some remains survive, including the Mudejar gate called "Puerta de la Magdalena" or "Puerta del Palacio de María de Molina". The fortified gate shows Mudejar features: an exterior horseshoe arch, a bent entrance (i.e., turned to make direct entry difficult) and two chambers inside that probably served as guard booths.

The castle is located in the town of Tiedra, province of Valladolid. It stands on a hill that dominates the plain of the Montes Torozos, giving it a strategic defensive position. The first documentary mention of the castle or the tower of Tiedra dates back to the 11th century during the reign of King Sancho II of Castile, when he ordered El Cid to mediate with Infanta Urraca of Zamora for the delivery of the city of Zamora in exchange, among other goods, for the castle of Tiedra. In the 12th and 13th centuries the castle passed through various noble hands: in 1203 King Alfonso IX of León granted the tower and town of Tiedra to his wife Berenguela of Castile after the annulment of their marriage. In 1285 King Sancho IV of Castile granted the town with its tower to Pedro Álvarez de Asturias. The daughter of Pedro married Alfonso Téllez de Meneses, of the powerful Téllez de Meneses lineage, so the castle became part of that lordship. The oldest preserved part corresponds to the defensive tower or keep, dated to the late 12th or early 13th century. This square-plan tower, built in ashlar, has several floors: a basement-dungeon, vaulted intermediate levels and a roof terrace offering wide views over the plain.

The castle is located in Montealegre de Campos, province of Valladolid. Defensive constructions have been documented on the site since 967, within the disputes between the kingdoms of Castile and León. The castle rises strategically at the highest point of the hill, dominating the Tierra de Campos plain. The current building was ordered in the 13th century by Alfonso Téllez de Meneses, member of a powerful noble lineage. Later it passed to the Alburquerque lineage (Dukes of Alburquerque) and was involved in various noble struggles, such as those between Pedro I of Castile and supporters of Enrique de Trastámara. During the Castilian Revolt of the Communidades (1520–1521) it also played a defensive and refuge role. The Montealegre castle, belonging to the Téllez de Meneses lineage — maternal family of María de Molina — was one of the places linked to her childhood, as it formed part of the seigneurial environment in which she grew and was educated before her marriage to Sancho IV of Castile. It is one of the best preserved medieval fortresses in the province of Valladolid, both in state and visibility, dominating the surrounding landscape and remaining impregnable during its history. Architecturally it has an almost square or trapezoidal plan, with robust walls up to 4–5 metres thick. Three of its corners have rectangular towers, while the fourth features the keep, with a pentagonal plan typical of 14th-century Castilian fortresses. The tower reaches about 20 metres high, from where the Montes Torozos plain can be seen.
C. Nicolás Rodríguez, 1, 47816 Montealegre de Campos, Valladolid

The monastery is located outside the medieval city walls, on the site of the former palace of the founding queen, near the La Magdalena suburb. Its establishment is linked to Queen María de Molina, who around 1282 ceded her own palace to found a Cistercian monastery under the invocation of Santa María la Real de las Huelgas. Shortly before her death, María de Molina requested in her will to be buried in this monastery. In 1328 the monastery was partially destroyed by a fire resulting from the repression of the city by royal troops. The church has a Latin-cross plan inscribed in a rectangle, with a single nave divided into bays and lateral chapels between buttresses. Notable interior works include the tomb of María de Molina in the centre of the transept, carved in alabaster with an effigy of the queen recumbent and decorative reliefs bearing the shields of the House of Burgundy represented by two castles and two lions (the lions borne crowned from the time of Sancho IV). Also notable is the tomb she inherited from her father Alfonso de Molina, a lion without a crown framed by several castles. The main altarpiece was designed by Francisco de Praves, with sculptures by Gregorio Fernández (≈1613) and paintings by Tomás de Prado.

Hello! I\'m María de Molina and I\'m going to tell you my story.
My parents were Infante Alfonso de Molina and Doña Mayor de Meneses.
Usual residence of María de Molina.
When I was 15, a prince named Sancho fell in love with me.
Later we moved to Valladolid to live in Sancho\'s palace.
When Sancho\'s father died, Sancho was chosen as King of Castile and León, and I became Queen.
During the reign, I helped Sancho fight in many battles.
Years later Sancho fell ill and died. I managed to have my son Fernando named king.
Fernando was still young and I helped him rule until he came of age.
Fernando was a good king but later died; I helped rule on behalf of my grandson Alfonso when he was too young.
Before dying I asked to be buried in the monastery of Santa María La Real de Huelgas.
You can tell if it will rain from my tomb because spots appear on it hours before. But be careful… if you touch them it stings!
Also, figures of a lizard, a monk covering his ears and a monster are hidden on my tomb. Try to find them!
